newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zairean rebel leader ready for push on Kinshasa.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebel leader ready for push on Kinshasa.

text.p: Rebel leader Laurent Kabila has said he has recruited 100,000 new guerrillas and is ready to open a fresh front for a final push to dislodge Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko from the capital Kinshasa.

"It won't take long. We'll be in Kinshasa very soon. We're only 200 km (120 miles) away from Kinshasa," Kabila told a rally on Saturday in Zaire's second city of Lubumbashi, seized by his rebels just over a week ago.

"In Bas Zaire Province, 100,000 young men have joined our cause," Kabila said, confirming widespread rumours in Kinshasa that rebel forces were grouping in western Zaire in a move to cut Kinshasa from its only access to the sea.

The vast Central African state's only seaport is situated in the province at Matadi on a small Atlantic coastline. It is the site of the country's lifeblood oil refinery and the gateway for most imported goods.

Kabila's announcement, even if exaggerated in terms of the number of recruits, looked certain to put more pressure on Mobutu, who has grudgingly agreed to meet the guerrilla leader in a desperate bid to negotiate an end to the six-month civil war.
Kinshasa is the last stronghold of Mobutu and his ragged government army. The rebels now control about half the sprawling country.
South Africa last week finally persuaded Mobutu to meet Kabila for the direct negotiations the rebel leader has long demanded as a way of ending the war.
But diplomats are sceptical about Kabila's interest in reaching any compromise given his overwhelming military advantage on the ground.
Zaire's lively press has speculated that Kabila might open a western front in the war to gain a shortcut to Kinshasa. He began his guerrilla campaign in Zaire's eastern provinces.

Bas Zaire (Lower Zaire) borders Angola whose government has been cited in recent Belgian press reports as backing Kabila, apparently in revenge for Mobutu's support of Angolan UNITA rebels during the southern African nation's own civil war.

An Angolan government aircraft was parked at Lubumbashi's airport on Friday and half a dozen heavily-armed, Portuguese-speaking commandos in spotless camouflage uniforms stayed the night at the city's main hotel, witnesses said.
They wore no insignia, shoulder flashes or badges of rank but looked like crack troops.
Mobutu's loyal political associates urged Western powers on Saturday to use their influence to secure a truce to pave the way for elections instead of pressing the president to step aside.
Kabila told the rally of some 10,000 people in Lubumbashi that there would be no compromise -- Mobutu and his hangers-on must go.
"We have to put all of Mobutu's people out of power so they can never raise their heads again," he said.

The rebel leader said that when stability and the rule of law had been established there would be "open elections in which every party could run for office -- except individuals who stole with Mobutu."
Since taking up arms last October to end Mobutu's 32-year rule, the rebels have met little resistance from the poorly-trained, unpaid and demoralised government army.
The army's penchant for looting and terrorising the local population has ensured the rebels were welcomed in town after town as liberators.
Public demonstrations of support for Kabila have also taken place in Kinshasa.
The rebels have seized Zaire's most important cities outside the capital as well as the richest mining provinces.
